claim_boundary: A rise in the IMF monthly global copper benchmark can reflect industrial demand, supply disruptions, dollar movements, inventories or speculative expectations. Exactly one preregistered long-or-cash audit may test whether the conservatively delayed three-month direction has matched-capital BTC value; no causal or alpha claim is imported from the sources.

primary_sources.identity: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis FRED, Global price of Copper [PCOPPUSDM]
primary_sources.evidence: The IMF-sourced series is monthly, not seasonally adjusted, in nominal U.S. dollars per metric ton, and represents period-average benchmark prices for the global market.
primary_sources.boundary: FRED exposes a present-vintage transport and explicitly notes that observations are subject to revision; it does not establish real-time vintage availability or future Bitcoin returns.

primary_sources.identity: International Monetary Fund Primary Commodity Prices FAQ
primary_sources.evidence: IMF documents monthly period-average nominal U.S.-dollar benchmark prices, a first-full-week publication cadence, and possible retroactive changes.
primary_sources.boundary: The documented release cadence supports a conservative availability lag but cannot remove present-vintage revision risk.

primary_sources.identity: International Monetary Fund, End of the Supercycle and Growth of Commodity Producers
primary_sources.evidence: The paper associates long copper cycles with global demand booms while also modelling China growth, the dollar, market expectations and real rates as copper-price drivers.
primary_sources.boundary: Copper direction is not a pure global-growth signal and its transmission to Bitcoin is unproven.

adversarial_prior: Copper prices can rise because of supply shocks or inflation pressure rather than stronger real activity or risk appetite.
Nominal U.S.-dollar copper direction can be dominated by broad-dollar movements already represented by a permanently closed family.
Energy-transition demand, inventories and speculative positioning can break a stable relation between copper direction and Bitcoin returns.
Monthly period averages and present-vintage revisions make precise real-time availability and historical replicability weaker than exchange-native data.
prohibited_rescue: Do not add copper inventories, futures curves, China data, the dollar, equities, oil, inflation, BTC trend, volatility or on-chain inputs.
Do not change the three-month horizon, direction, 75-day availability floor, threshold, sizing or parent after source or outcome access.
Do not reinterpret the closed WTI, broad-dollar, China-FX, liquidity or macro-activity families as support for this one.

independence.distinct_from_closed_gold_volatility: This is the direction of a physical industrial-metal benchmark, not implied volatility or a precious-metal calm-state filter.
independence.distinct_from_closed_wti: Copper has different end-use demand, supply and inventory structure from crude oil; no oil input or rescue is allowed.
independence.distinct_from_closed_fx_and_us_macro: The decision input is a global copper benchmark only, not an exchange rate or a U.S. activity release. Confounding by those variables remains an adversarial risk, not an added feature.

missing_proof: No exact 2018-2024 response, date lattice, missing-value audit, revision-safe vintage or conservative availability mapping has been sealed.
No state support, transition support, hypothesis, manifest, runner, fees, slippage, PnL, drawdown, holding, inventory, breadth, concentration, candidate, OOS or forward evidence exists.
